article_title: Simulating Interference and Diffraction in Instructional Laboratories
citation: Leon N. Maurer. (2012). Simulating Interference and Diffraction in Instructional Laboratories. https://arxiv.org/abs/1208.1027
title: Interference-Inference-Interface: an interactive FDTD simulation for quantitative measurement of interference and diffraction
description: A Python program using the Finite Difference Time Domain method that simulates interference and diffraction with interactive, animated waves and "easily measured amplitudes at any user desired grid point". It displays Ez and EzRMS plots with movable crosshair lines, lets users add, remove and modify barrier openings, uses split-field perfectly matched layers to reduce reflections to imperceptible levels, and includes a fast forward mode. Executables, source code (GNU Public License version 2), and program information are available at the project website.
requirements: Runs on Windows, OS X, and Linux using NumPy, TkInter, and the Python Imaging Library; laboratory computers achieved smooth animation at approximately 55ms per timestep
constraints: A 2D simulation in which amplitude falls off less quickly than in 3D; discretization can slightly alter the interference conditions; the domain is too small to truly display far field effects
target_learners: introductory calculus-based physics students, aimed at future physics majors
target_learning_goals: conditions for constructive and destructive interference
examples: Students used it to find four maxima and four minima of EzRMS in the double-slit simulation, calculate |d0−d1|λ for each, and find the pattern in those numbers
key_sources: Leon N. Maurer. (2012). Simulating Interference and Diffraction in Instructional Laboratories. https://arxiv.org/abs/1208.1027

article_title: Functional data analysis of college students' sleep patterns and their relationships with academic performance and social networks: A four-year longitudinal study.
citation: Zhao Yao, Zhou Haoyu. (2026). Functional data analysis of college students’ sleep patterns and their relationships with academic performance and social networks: A four-year longitudinal study. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0351120
title: Functional data analysis pipeline for modeling sleep as a continuous four-year trajectory
description: This element is the study's analytical apparatus: daily Fitbit sleep minutes are converted into smooth continuous functions using cubic B-spline basis functions (order 4), with the number of basis functions chosen by generalized cross-validation and knots placed at semester boundaries. Concurrent functional linear regression with roughness-penalty smoothing estimates time-varying sleep–GPA coefficients, and pointwise functional t-tests with permutation testing compare sleep curves between social-activity groups. The authors present FDA as "particularly well-suited for examining continuous temporal processes in naturalistic settings", revealing dynamics that discrete-time analyses would miss.
requirements: Participants need sufficient temporal coverage for stable B-spline estimation; the study required sleep data for at least 50% of the study period (678 of 1,356 possible days)
constraints: The authors do not claim FDA is universally superior to mixed-effects or growth-curve models; they recommend selecting analytical approaches based on the specific research question and data characteristics
target_learning_goals: understanding longitudinal sleep behavior and its relationship to academic performance
examples: The U-shaped sleep–GPA coefficient pattern, which the authors state would be invisible to analyses using yearly or semester averages
key_sources: Zhao Yao, Zhou Haoyu. (2026). Functional data analysis of college students’ sleep patterns and their relationships with academic performance and social networks: A four-year longitudinal study. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0351120
